vignette:
At 70, Meera Patel had spent most of her adult life behind a camera, preferring to frame other people’s faces rather than place her own in view. She grew up in an immigrant South Asian family in the United States and was physically abused by a caregiver throughout childhood, most often inside the home where there was no witness and, in her mind, no protection. She described being grabbed, struck, and cornered by an adult whose moods seemed to change without warning. What stayed with her was not only the pain but the helplessness of watching the person who was supposed to care for her become dangerous while the rest of the family carried on as if nothing had happened. Even now, when she speaks about that period, she returns to the fact that the people responsible were never held to account. She had come to believe that this was how the world worked: harm could be done to a child and simply disappear into silence.

That belief hardened over the years into a broader sense that she did not really belong anywhere. Meera was divorced, lived alone, and described moving through social spaces with the feeling of being fundamentally outside them, as if other people had been issued some membership card to safety and she had not. In her work as a photographer, she could function well enough as long as she stayed in control of the interaction, but she remained acutely watchful. During portrait sessions she tracked changes in tone, posture, and expression with exhausting intensity, scanning clients and assistants for signs of irritation or unpredictability. She was certain she had to stay on guard all the time. That same conviction shaped how she managed herself: she tried hard to control her emotions, kept her face still, and when she felt herself becoming exposed she would cover her face with her hands, a gesture that felt both protective and reflexive. She also found herself circling the old question of why this had happened to her, turning it over privately for hours without arriving at relief.

Those efforts did not bring clarity. The more Meera tried to contain herself and make sense of the abuse, the more unstable the memories felt when they came. If she attempted to deliberately remember specific incidents, her mind seemed to go blank around the middle of them; she could approach the edge of a scene but not hold onto it in an orderly way. Yet when something pierced that distance, the memories arrived with the same terror she had felt as a child, immediate and bodily, and with an intense rush of shame that made her want to hide her face. In session she described a familiar pattern: she would begin trying to think through what had happened and why, clamp down on tears and panic, and then suddenly feel overtaken by fragments that were unbearable rather than understandable. Her attempts to master the emotion left her dreading the memory even more.

This had become more visible in the past year because her work increasingly put her in situations she could not fully choreograph. During a family photo shoot, an older client lifted his hand sharply to call to a grandson across the room. Meera knew, rationally, that nothing was happening to her, but the movement hit her like a blow. In an instant she felt the old terror in her chest and heat in her face, and shame followed so quickly that she half turned away and covered her face with her hands under the pretense of adjusting her camera strap. Afterward she spent the evening asking herself again why this had happened to her and why no one had ever answered for it. The more convinced she became that the world was still a place where people could harm and get away with it, and that she had no real place of safety with others, the more tightly she tried to police every sign of feeling. At work she shortened sessions, avoided collaborative shoots, and kept conversations clipped so no one would notice when her expression changed.

Over weeks and months, that vigilance narrowed her life. She took fewer jobs that involved families or children because she could not bear the unpredictability of intimate dynamics in the room. She kept acquaintances at a distance and rarely let anyone photograph her. What frightened her most was not only the memory itself but the possibility that if she stopped controlling herself, the terror and shame would break through in front of other people and confirm what she already feared—that she was marked by something that left her apart. She finally sought help after leaving a session early when she could not recover her composure following another sudden gesture from a client. Meera said she was tired of living as if danger were always about to step into the frame. She wants, cautiously, to understand why the memories still have this force, but she is afraid that looking directly at them will bring back the same terror and shame she has spent a lifetime trying to hide.
